blocks.markdown: Eleven exceptions: four from the statute, seven recognized later

RA 1405 itself names four exceptions. Later laws and jurisprudence add seven more: AMLC inquiry under the AMLA, three BIR inquiry paths under the Tax Code, PDIC/BSP inquiry on unsafe-practice findings, unclaimed-balances disclosure and escheat, and garnishment of peso deposits. That makes eleven — the number examiners expect. This lesson walks them in that order, then shows what looks like an exception but is not (the Ombudsman, general BSP examination), and closes with penalties.

The four, with their case anchors: **(1) Written permission of the depositor** — the depositor's own consent, the model for all waivers (including DOSRI waivers). **(2) Impeachment** — inquiry in an impeachment case needs no depositor consent. **(3) Court order in bribery or dereliction-of-duty cases** against public officials — covers plunder and unexplained wealth as the same class (Ejercito, citing PNB v. Gancayco). **(4) Money deposited is the subject matter of the litigation** — the money itself must be the thing in dispute (Union Bank), reaching accounts it was allegedly transferred to (Ejercito). In-camera inspection additionally requires a pending court case, an identified account, limited scope, and notice (Marquez).
The subject-matter exception, fenced in

The Union Bank test: ask what the lawsuit is really about. If the plaintiff says 'that money in that account is mine or was stolen from me,' the money itself is the subject matter and inquiry is allowed. If the plaintiff says 'you owe me damages and I measure them at P999,000,' the account is just where payment might come from — no inquiry. Application: a company suing its treasurer to recover embezzled funds deposited in his personal account falls inside the exception; a company suing a supplier for breach-of-contract damages does not get to browse the supplier's accounts.
Bribery, dereliction, and plunder

Ejercito teaches a two-exception analysis for corruption prosecutions. First, bribery/dereliction is read by class: plunder and unexplained-wealth cases belong with bribery because public office is a public trust (the Court adopts PNB v. Gancayco's reasoning). Second, subject matter follows the money: once tainted funds are allegedly moved to another account — even in another person's name — that account holds the subject matter too. Combine both and a Sandiganbayan subpoena in a plunder case is doubly supported. Remember the pairing: Union Bank fences the exception in, Ejercito shows how far inside that fence it still reaches.
AMLA inquiry: the AMLC pathway

Verified summary of the current rule (AMLA Sec. 11 as amended by RA 10167, untouched by RA 10365 and RA 11521): the AMLC may inquire into or examine any particular deposit or investment, including related accounts, **notwithstanding RA 1405, RA 6426, RA 8791, and other laws** — upon court order based on an ex parte application showing probable cause linking the funds to an unlawful activity or money laundering. **No court order** is needed for kidnapping-for-ransom, dangerous-drugs, and hijacking/destructive-arson/murder predicates (Sec. 3(i)(1), (2), (12)), similar felonies punishable abroad, and terrorism. Related accounts need their own ex parte order. Full AMLA procedure belongs to the AMLA module (bank-inquiry topic); what matters here is that the 'notwithstanding' clause makes this a true secrecy override reaching even foreign currency deposits.
BIR inquiry: three paths, no more

Three exclusive paths, each with a control: **(1) Decedent** — inquiry only to determine the gross estate for estate tax; the death itself opens the account. **(2) Compromise applicant** — a taxpayer pleading financial incapacity must first waive secrecy in writing, or the application is not even considered; the waiver itself becomes the Commissioner's authority. **(3) Treaty request** — a specific taxpayer named in a foreign tax authority's request under a tax convention, with the information then usable for BIR assessment, verification, audit, and enforcement. The 'notwithstanding RA 1405 and RA 6426' lead-in means peso and foreign currency deposits alike are reached. Accountancy angle: estate-tax work routinely touches path (1); compromise practice lives or dies on the path (2) waiver.

Trap: a routine BIR audit of a living taxpayer does NOT authorize opening deposit records. No decedent, no compromise-plus-waiver, no treaty request — no inquiry. The bank must refuse, and the examiner must build the assessment from returns, invoices, and third-party data instead.
PDIC and BSP inquiry on unsafe practices

The trigger is everything: inquiry is allowed only **in case there is a finding of fraud or unsafe or unsound banking related to deposit-taking**. On that finding, the PDIC and/or the BSP may examine deposit accounts and all related information despite RA 1405, RA 6426, and RA 8791, while reusing BSP reports to avoid duplication. In practice this is how ailing banks get opened up — examiners trace fictitious, fraudulent, or unsafe-practice deposits — but a healthy bank under routine supervision stays sealed.
Unclaimed balances: disclose to escheat

The moving parts around the quoted report duty: **'Unclaimed balances'** (Sec. 1) means credits or deposits — money, bullion, securities, or other evidence of indebtedness plus interest — favoring someone known to be dead or with no deposit or withdrawal for **ten years or more**. After the sworn report and 60-day posting, the **Treasurer tells the Solicitor General, who files an escheat action** joining the bank and the depositors, with published summons and notice (Sec. 3). A bank that misses the report pays **P500 per month** of default (Sec. 4); one that duly turns balances over is **discharged** and defended by the OSG free of charge (Sec. 5). Dormant-account work in banks and audit confirmations both brush against this law.
Garnishment of peso deposits

Ortega's reasoning is the whole answer pattern for garnishment questions: execution of a final judgment is not an 'inquiry' at all, and confirming that the money sits in the account discloses nothing beyond what execution needs. Business consequence: a company's operating deposits are reachable by a winning creditor — secrecy protects against snooping, not against lawful collection. Contrast this immediately with foreign currency deposits, which Sec. 8 of RA 6426 expressly shields from garnishment (next lesson; Salvacion is the narrow equitable exception).
What is NOT an exception

Marquez draws the court's line vs the investigator's line: a court with a pending bribery, plunder, or subject-matter case may order inquiry (Ejercito), but an Ombudsman armed only with an investigation may not — RA 6770's 'access to bank accounts' language does not override RA 1405. Pair this with the in-camera safeguards (pending case, identified account, limited scope, notice to bank and holder) for a complete answer. Any question dangling Ombudsman subpoena power as a secrecy exception is testing whether you say no.

Read the tail clause — 'subject to' secrecy laws — and the common error disappears: regular or special BSP examination of a bank does NOT carry a standing right to open deposit accounts. Since PD 1792's repeal there is no fraud-examination exception inside RA 1405; examination-related inquiry needs its own basis, namely the PDIC Charter's Eighth power (unsafe-practice finding) or the depositor's waiver, such as the DOSRI waiver below. If an exam choice lists 'BSP examination' as a blanket exception, it is the wrong choice.

The DOSRI waiver is best understood as a statutory application of the written-permission exception: the insider's own signed waiver opens only his own deposits, above the threshold, to examiners — and even then the information stays strictly confidential and usable only for supervision or a BSP-initiated action on the account. It does not open other depositors' accounts, and it does not authorize public disclosure. Lending to DOSRI accounts is also a related-party-transaction red flag auditors watch, which is why the waiver exists.
Penalties

Two numbers to memorize: **five years** and **twenty thousand pesos** — both ceilings ('not more than'), imposable singly or together at the court's discretion, and only **upon conviction**. The penalty attaches to 'any violation of this law,' which in practice means unlawful disclosure under Section 3. Compare: RA 6426 punishes willful violations with one to five years and P5,000-P25,000 (floors and ceilings), while unclaimed-balances reporting default costs P500 per month administratively.

table.caption: The eleven exceptions at a glance
rows: Court order in bribery/dereliction cases (incl. plunder, unexplained wealth)
Money deposited is the subject matter of the litigation
AMLC inquiry (court order; no order for Sec. 3(i)(1), (2), (12), similar foreign felonies, terrorism)
BIR inquiry into a decedent's deposits (gross estate)
BIR inquiry into a compromise applicant's deposits (written waiver required)
BIR inquiry for a foreign tax authority treaty request
PDIC/BSP inquiry on finding of unsafe or unsound banking practice
Garnishment of peso deposits to satisfy a judgment

blocks.markdown: Remember: answer exception questions in layers — (1) is it one of the four in Section 2? (2) if not, is it a later-law pathway with its own procedure? (3) if neither, the answer is no, and say which safeguard is missing (no court order, no pending case, no waiver, no finding). Name the non-exceptions explicitly: Ombudsman investigation, general BSP examination, and routine BIR audit open nothing.
☐ Can I recite all eleven exceptions with one authority each?
☐ Can I explain why Ombudsman investigation, general BSP examination, and routine BIR audit are not exceptions?
